description: We are a team of girls from the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU - Brazil), passionate about programming, game development, and web technologies. We are excited to combine creativity and technology to explore challenges and spark curiosity through our projects.
summary:
Mars Academy is an educational and interactive game aimed at children, in which the player takes on the role of an astronaut and must survive for ten days on Mars after Earth collapses.
The game addresses the challenge of survival on the Red Planet by placing the child at the center of decision-making. During the mission, they must manage six vital indicators (oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health) while exploring the environment, completing nighttime tasks to collect items, and facing time-limited emergencies. All of this is integrated with educational explanations and real space phenomena, using official NASA sources and solar activity data from the NASA DONKI API.
This project is important because it teaches children to think critically, manage scarce resources, and understand the consequences of their own choices. In addition to sparking interest in science and space exploration in a fun way, the story reinforces an essential message about the importance of caring for and preserving planet Earth by understanding the difficulties we would face on another planet.
details:
Mars Academy is an educational game of survival, decision-making, and minigames aimed at children aged 7 to 12, also designed for use by teachers in the classroom. The application runs directly in the browser on computers, tablets, and smartphones, with each playthrough lasting an estimated 10 to 20 minutes.

Play the game online here: https://mars-academy.lovable.app/
Check out the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Maryendlu/Nasa-Space-Apps-Lovelace

The narrative takes place in the year 2045, in a scenario where Earth faces crises of environmental degradation, climate change, and resource scarcity. To address this reality, NASA creates Project New Horizon and sends four astronauts to Mars on a ten-day expedition. Shortly after landing, communication with Earth begins to fail, meaning the support team can only arrive on the tenth day. The player takes on the role of Maya — a specialist in astronomy and natural sciences — or Milo — focused on technology, robotics, and exploration — young astronauts-in-training participating in the mission through a NASA simulation. Throughout the journey, the team is accompanied by three specialists: Andreas, an aerospace engineer responsible for energy, equipment, and life support; Laika, a biologist and astrobiologist in charge of water, soil, climate, and cultivation; and Lina, a space physician focused on health, nutrition, and radiation.

The gameplay is divided into daytime and nighttime periods. During the day, one of the specialists presents a real Martian problem, such as dust storms, water scarcity, oxygen failures, excess carbon dioxide, among others. The player has three action alternatives, none of which are perfect; protecting a specific resource always comes at the cost of another, requiring choices based on logic and consequences that are followed by scientific explanations. Survival is monitored by six indicators that start at 70: oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health. Of these, radiation never decreases, so decisions aim solely to avoid adding risk levels. At night, the player explores the base and can complete up to three of nine optional minigames, such as reconnecting circuits, restarting the oxygen generator, and cleaning solar panels. Each minigame shares real NASA trivia, and any failures result only in the loss of the reward. Additionally, on random nights, surprise emergencies occur — such as pressure loss, battery fires, and water contamination — triggering an alarm with a 30-to-45-second timer; if time runs out, the mission is immediately terminated. A playthrough can end in three distinct outcomes: mission completed successfully, completed with difficulties, or terminated if oxygen, water, or health reaches zero or radiation reaches one hundred, displaying at the end a logbook with all choices for joint reflection.

The project accurately addresses the challenge of creating a mission trainer for young astronauts by proposing real trade-offs in every decision, integrating with real space weather through queries to the NASA DONKI API, maintaining full data transparency via a space weather dashboard, simulating the real signal delay between Mars and Earth through the Deep Space Network, ensuring high replayability, and providing pedagogical guidelines for teachers. The game's impact encompasses social awareness regarding the urgency of caring for our planet — reinforced by the final message "Teach the children. Shape the future. Save the Earth" —, the stimulation of critical thinking, prioritization, and resource management in education, and bringing children closer to real science and space agency technologies, such as MOXIE, Perseverance, and life support systems.

Regarding the technological resources and tools used in development, TypeScript was the main programming language utilized, while HTML and CSS structured the visuals and screen layouts. The storage of the storyline, choices, translations, and scientific sources was handled in JSON files. The screens and interactivity were built with React, using TanStack Start and Router for navigation, Vite for project execution and bundling, and Tailwind CSS for design and animations. Automated tests for game rules, emergencies, inventory, and languages were executed with Vitest, and code editing was handled in VS Code. Real-world data was obtained through the NASA DONKI API and other sources cited in the credits, while the soundtrack was sourced from Pixabay.com. We also used Artificial Intelligence tools, such as Lovable and Claude, to support technical implementation, assisting in generating and organizing code, building the interface, and creating images and videos. The project requires no special hardware, running smoothly in browsers on computers, tablets, and smartphones.

All decisions regarding the concept, script, in-game choices, aesthetics/design, player experience, objectives, mechanics, and solution validation were led entirely by our team, which also reviewed and adapted all content generated by AI tools to accelerate development without replacing the creative participation of the team members. Throughout the process, we primarily considered the target age group, striving to create an accessible, intuitive, and fun experience for children. We also prioritized the scientific accuracy of the information (based on NASA sources), the balance between difficulty and learning, continuous engagement throughout the entire game, and building an attractive visual interface and compelling narrative.
